definition: Candid means honest and open — saying what you actually think, uncomfortable parts included, without rehearsal or disguise.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word candid. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know candid should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Her application essay worked because it was candid: instead of polishing her record, she wrote about the semester she nearly quit, and why.
Honest is the milder rung: an honest answer avoids falsehood but may stop right there, while a candid one volunteers the uncomfortable parts nobody asked about.
Blunt is stronger than candid: candid opens the whole ledger but still minds the listener, while blunt drops it on the table, careless of what it bruises.

Frank and candid both hand over the unvarnished truth, but frank leans on the delivery of one plain statement — a frank assessment, a frank refusal. Candid describes the whole open posture: nothing rehearsed, nothing held in reserve, the speaker plain in every word.

Outspoken is candor with the volume up — opinions offered freely, invited or not, sometimes to the room's discomfort. Candid answers openly when the truth is called for; it doesn't need a soapbox, only a real question.

The reviewer's incandescent praise ran two full columns and sold out the play's first month by Friday.
Candid means honest and open — saying what you actually think, uncomfortable parts included, without rehearsal or disguise.
The recipe site thrived on candid reviews: beneath the glossy photographs, home cooks reported the sauce that curdled, the timing that ran long, and the cheap substitution that worked better.
Candid speech volunteers the inconvenient part.
A polite review could have praised the photography and moved on; a candid one says what the cook actually found, failures included — openness offered freely, not extracted under questioning.
Candid is honesty with the door open — unrehearsed, complete, and offered rather than extracted.
It is warmer than blunt, which tells the truth without caring where it lands, and straighter than diplomatic speech, which re-tailors the truth to please its hearer.
Photographers use it the same way: a candid shot is one nobody staged.
This unit already gave you the noun — candor is the quality, candid the person or the remark — and forthright, its close unit-mate, leans harder on directness where candid leans on openness.
